title: The Old Silk Route via Zuluk: A Practical Guide
meta_description: Plan East Sikkim's Old Silk Route: Rongli permits, Padamchen and Zuluk homestays, Thambi loops, Lungthung sunrise, Gnathang and Kupup, with costs and seasons.
summary: The Old Silk Route climbs from Rongli through Padamchen and Zuluk to Gnathang and Kupup, on the mule road that once carried Tibetan wool over Jelep La. Plan two or three nights, a Rongli permit and a reserved SUV at ₹5,000–7,000 a day, or shared jeeps to Rongli on a budget. Homestays cost ₹1,200–2,200 per person with meals.

sections.heading: What the Silk Route is, and is not
paras: The name is a modern one. In its working life this was a wool road: from Kalimpong to Pedong, Rhenock and Rongli, then up through the forest to Zuluk, over Jelep La at 4,390 m and down into Tibet's Chumbi valley. Mule trains carried wool south to Kalimpong's warehouses and took cloth, salt, tools and tea north. In 1888 British and Tibetan forces fought on this ridge, clashing at Gnathang on 22 May. The trade thinned after 1959 and stopped when the border was sealed after the 1962 war.

Today the army road, signed NH717B, follows the old line in dozens of hairpin bends, and family homestays in Padamchen, Zuluk and Gnathang have opened to travellers. It is not a trek and not a luxury trip. It is a slow drive through forest, rhododendron and high grassland, with cold nights in simple homes and, on clear mornings, Kanchenjunga on the western horizon. You need a permit, a sturdy car and spare time for weather.

sections.heading: The route, stop by stop
paras: Distances and heights are approximate. Gangtok to Rongli is about 69 km, and Rongli to Zuluk about 32 km. The road beyond Zuluk climbs steeply to above 3,900 m within an hour or two.

sections.heading: How many nights, and in what order
paras: Two nights is the comfortable minimum. Drive from Gangtok to Zuluk on day one, with lunch and the permit at Rongli. On day two, rise at 4 am for the Lungthung sunrise, stop at Thambi View Point on the way down for the loops in morning light, then drive up again to Gnathang and Kupup and come back to Zuluk. On day three, drive down to Rongli and on to Gangtok, Aritar or Siliguri.

Three nights is better, and the way we prefer it. Sleep the first night at Padamchen, at about 2,000 m, so your body adjusts before Zuluk; then two nights at Zuluk, giving you two chances at a clear dawn. Some travellers add a night at Gnathang, at around 3,900 m, which is beautiful and very cold, but only after a night at Zuluk and only if everyone feels well. Many combine the Silk Route with Aritar, about an hour from Rongli, for a gentler lake night at 1,400 m.
Avoid doing the whole route as a long day trip from Gangtok. It rushes the altitude, misses the dawn, and spends most of the day in a car.

sections.heading: Getting there and getting around
paras: Most travellers hire a reserved SUV for the whole trip from Gangtok or Siliguri, at about ₹5,000–7,000 a day, with the driver arranging the permit in advance. From Siliguri the drive to Zuluk is about 140–150 km and 5–6 hours via Rangpo and Rongli. When NH10 along the Teesta is closed, as it often has been since the October 2023 flood, cars come up through Kalimpong or Lava, Pedong and Rhenock instead, the old trade route itself. Check current status before you travel.

On a budget, take a shared jeep from Gangtok to Rongli, about 2.5–3 hours, for ₹200–300 a seat. Collect your permit there, then go up the last 32 km in a car your homestay sends. For the high road beyond Zuluk you still need a vehicle; homestays can arrange a sunrise and Kupup round trip, and solo travellers can sometimes share with other guests. Carry cash: there is no ATM we would rely on beyond Rongli.

sections.heading: Permits and paperwork
paras: Indian travellers need a Silk Route permit, issued at Rongli. Your homestay or driver usually applies in advance with scanned copies of your photo ID and passport photos, and the permit is collected as you pass through Rongli. It should list where you will stay. Whether you can continue from Kupup past Baba Mandir to Tsomgo and Gangtok, completing a loop, depends on the permit and army rules of the season; ask before you plan around it.

Foreign nationals need the Sikkim Restricted Area Permit and a further permit through a registered agency, and access for foreigners to the Silk Route has changed several times, sometimes closing altogether. Ask a registered Gangtok agency well ahead. Carry photocopies of ID and spare photos. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Altitude, cold and safety
paras: The Silk Route climbs fast. From Rongli at under 1,000 m you can reach Kupup at about 4,000 m in a day, which is how altitude sickness happens. Sleep at Padamchen or Zuluk before going higher, drink plenty of water, avoid alcohol on the first night, and go down if anyone has a severe headache, vomiting, confusion or breathlessness at rest. Take medical advice before travelling with infants or anyone with heart or lung conditions.

Nights are cold for most of the year: near freezing at Zuluk from November to March, and well below at Gnathang and Kupup. Homestays give heavy blankets, but bring thermals, a down jacket, a warm hat, gloves and thick socks. Snow can close the road between Zuluk and Kupup for days from December to March. In the monsoon, from June to September, slides are frequent and views rare; we suggest avoiding it.
list: Carry a basic medical kit and any prescription medicines.
Mobile signal is patchy beyond Rongli; tell family your plans.
Respect army rules: no photography of camps or soldiers.
Pack out your rubbish; there is little waste collection up here.

sections.heading: What it costs
paras: For two people sharing a reserved SUV, a two-night Silk Route trip from Gangtok usually costs about ₹14,000–20,000 in all, of which the car is ₹10,000–14,000. Homestays charge ₹1,200–2,200 per person a night with dinner and breakfast. Tea costs ₹20–40, a bowl of thukpa ₹100–180, and hired boots or a warm coat ₹100–200 a day in winter. Permit charges are small, though agents and homestays may add a fee for arranging them. A solo traveller using shared jeeps to Rongli and sharing high-road trips can manage on ₹2,500–3,500 a day. Prices are indicative for 2025–26.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for the Silk Route?
faqs.a: Two nights is the comfortable minimum: one in Zuluk to adjust, a dawn trip to Lungthung and a day to Gnathang and Kupup, then the drive out. Three nights, with a first night at Padamchen and two at Zuluk, is better for acclimatisation and gives two chances at a clear sunrise.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for the Silk Route?
faqs.a: Yes. Indian travellers need a Silk Route permit issued at Rongli, usually arranged in advance by a homestay or driver with scanned photo ID and photos. Foreigners need the Sikkim Restricted Area Permit and a further permit via a registered agency, and their access has varied. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time for the Silk Route?
faqs.a: October and November give the clearest views of Kanchenjunga and the Zuluk loops. April and May bring rhododendrons and longer days. December to March brings snow, which is beautiful but can close the road for days. June to September is the monsoon, with landslides and cloud, and we suggest avoiding it.

faqs.q: How much does a Silk Route trip cost?
faqs.a: For two people, a two-night trip from Gangtok costs about ₹14,000–20,000 in all, mostly the reserved SUV at ₹5,000–7,000 a day. Homestays charge ₹1,200–2,200 per person with meals. Solo travellers using shared jeeps to Rongli can manage on ₹2,500–3,500 a day. Prices are indicative for 2025–26.

faqs.q: Can I do the Silk Route by shared jeep?
faqs.a: Partly. Shared jeeps run from Gangtok to Rongli for ₹200–300 a seat. Beyond Rongli there is no regular shared transport, so your homestay sends a car for the last 32 km to Zuluk, and you need a vehicle for the sunrise and the high road. Solo travellers can sometimes share these trips.

faqs.q: Is the Silk Route safe for children and older people?
faqs.a: Zuluk, at about 2,900 m, suits healthy families and older travellers who go slowly. The high road climbs to about 4,000 m, which is harder. Sleep lower first, keep everyone warm and hydrated, avoid the trip with infants, and take medical advice for heart or lung conditions. Turn back if anyone feels unwell.

faqs.q: Can I combine the Silk Route with Tsomgo Lake?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Some trips continue from Kupup past Baba Mandir to Tsomgo and down to Gangtok, but that crossing depends on the permits issued and army rules of the season, and is not always allowed. Ask your operator before booking, and have a backup plan of returning via Rongli.

faqs.q: Why is it called the Silk Route?
faqs.a: Travellers use the name for the old trade road from Kalimpong through Rongli and Zuluk over Jelep La into Tibet. In practice it carried mostly wool, along with salt, cloth and tea, rather than silk. The trade ended after the border closed in 1962. The name is loose, but it has stuck.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network on the Silk Route?
faqs.a: Signal is patchy beyond Rongli, often gone for hours in Zuluk, Gnathang and Kupup, and some homestays have none. Tell family your plans before you leave Rongli, download offline maps and carry cash, as there are no ATMs we would rely on above Rongli.
